analysis.one_liner: Lets cities, counties, and Indian tribes offer their own broadband even when state laws ban it.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had five cosponsors from both parties, never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal telecommunications law to say that no state could pass or keep a law preventing cities, counties, other local governments, or Indian tribes from offering high-speed internet service to residents and businesses. In the mid-2000s, several states had passed such bans, generally at the urging of cable and telephone companies that did not want public competition. The bill also included rules requiring city-owned networks to treat private competitors fairly and to follow the same state and federal telecom regulations as everyone else.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of towns and cities — especially areas with slow or expensive service and few providers — would gain a new option, because their local governments could build or offer broadband even where state law currently forbids it. Local governments and Indian tribes would gain the legal power to invest in their own networks.

how_it_helps.text: No state statute or regulation could prohibit or effectively prohibit any public provider — a state, a political subdivision, or an Indian tribe — from offering advanced telecommunications capability or services that use it.
City-owned networks would still be subject to the same federal and state telecommunications laws as private providers; the bill contained a savings clause to that effect.

Where a public provider regulates competing private providers, it would have to apply its rules without discriminating in favor of itself or any service it owns, and federal law would still let competing carriers interconnect with its network.

analysis.who_pays: Private cable and telephone broadband companies would face new public competition, which tends to push down prices in markets with only one or two providers. State governments would lose their authority to ban municipal networks. Local taxpayers could bear the cost if a city-funded network lost money.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private broadband providers and state governments

drawbacks.text: The bill's core purpose is to let government-owned networks compete with private firms, and critics of municipal broadband argue that public networks backed by taxpayer-backed financing can outcompete private companies not because they serve customers better but because they do not face the same market risks — and that local taxpayers can be left holding the losses if the network fails.

Even with its antidiscrimination safeguards, a city that is simultaneously a network operator and a regulator could still favor its own operation in practice, which is why the bill had to include rules against self-dealing in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households stuck with slow or expensive service and no alternative provider, the option of a locally run network is a genuine benefit, and the bill tried to address the fairness concerns by requiring equal treatment of competitors and applying all normal telecom regulation to public providers. The real cost risk is financial: municipal networks are funded with public money, and a badly run one could burden local taxpayers. On balance, the bill was a modest, targeted override of state bans rather than a subsidy program, and its safeguards were substantive.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 23, 2005, by Senator Frank Lautenberg of New Jersey, introduced on his behalf and that of Senator John McCain of Arizona.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
The committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the 109th Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
The bill never received a vote in either chamber of Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband providers are better off, because the markets they serve were never opened to competition from city-owned networks. State laws banning municipal broadband also stayed in place, since Congress did nothing to override them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent broadband providers; no one else

for.name: Sen. Frank Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip state legal power to block local governments and Indian tribes from offering broadband.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor; the bill was introduced 'for himself and Mr. McCain.'

against.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Cable and telephone broadband providers
against.what_they_did: Fought municipal broadband, including by supporting the state laws banning city-owned networks that this bill would have overridden.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — its five cosponsors included three Republicans and two Democrats — but since it never reached a floor vote, the parties' positions were never tested on the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have let city-owned networks compete with them directly, and where only one or two companies sell broadband, public competition tends to push prices down and push coverage into areas private firms have not built. These companies supported the state bans the bill would have voided.

industries.industry: Local governments, municipal utilities, and Indian tribes
industries.note: They would gain the legal authority to build and operate broadband networks for their residents, an option state law currently denies them in several states.
